title: WHY DID A HIGH PRIEST CHOOSE TWO WIVES FOR A YOUNG KING? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND A MARRIAGE ARRANGED IN THE HOUSE OF GOD
paragraphs: WHY DID A HIGH PRIEST CHOOSE TWO WIVES FOR A YOUNG KING? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND A MARRIAGE ARRANGED IN THE HOUSE OF GOD

He was rescued from a massacre, raised under a priest's protection, and given two wives while still young. But the most heartbreaking part of King Joash's story wasn't whom he married. It was whom he eventually betrayed. And buried inside this ancient account is a warning every Christian needs to hear before it's too late.
There is something deeply unsettling about a man who can spend years surrounded by the things of God… and still end up turning his back on God Himself.
He can know the Scriptures.
He can sit under godly leadership.
He can help restore a place of worship.
He can even become the answer to somebody else's prayers.
And still, somewhere beneath the appearance of faithfulness, there can be a heart that has never learned to stand before God without someone else holding it upright.
That is what makes the story of King Joash so frightening.
Because when you first meet him, you want him to succeed.
You want the little boy to survive.
You want the rescued child to become a righteous king.
You want the priest who protected him to live long enough to see everything turn out beautifully.
And for a while, it looks as though that is exactly what will happen.
Until you read what comes next.
But before we get to the betrayal, we need to answer the question that makes this passage so unusual.
Why would Jehoiada, the high priest of Judah, personally choose two wives for a young king?
And why would Scripture mention that decision immediately after describing Joash's obedience?
The answer takes us into a royal nursery stained by violence, a covenant nearly buried beneath political ambition, and a spiritual tragedy that reaches far beyond the palace walls.
It begins with a little boy who should have been dead.
His name was Joash.
And someone wanted him erased.
The story unfolds during one of the darkest periods in Judah's royal history.
After King Ahaziah died, his mother Athaliah seized power. According to 2 Kings 11:1 and 2 Chronicles 22:10, she began destroying the royal offspring.
Think about the horror of that.
These were not merely political rivals.
They were members of her own royal family.
Children whose lives stood between her and the throne.
The palace that should have protected them had become a place of death.
And somewhere in that nightmare was an infant named Joash.
Too young to understand the danger.
Too helpless to defend himself.
Too small to know that the royal blood running through his veins had made him a target.
But God had not abandoned the Davidic royal line.
A woman named Jehoshabeath, identified in Chronicles as the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, secretly rescued Joash and his nurse.
She hid them from Athaliah.
Then, for six years, Joash remained concealed while Athaliah ruled the land.
Six years.
Imagine the whispered conversations.
The guarded doors.
The fear that one careless movement might expose the child.
Imagine Jehoiada watching this little boy grow, knowing that his life was tied to the future of Judah's throne.
And behind that throne stood something greater than royal politics.
God had made a covenant with David.
In 2 Samuel 7:12–16, the Lord promised to establish David's royal house and kingdom, with a dynasty whose ultimate fulfillment would be found in Jesus Christ.
Psalm 89 also remembers God's covenant with David, even while acknowledging the painful reality of judgment upon unfaithful descendants.
The Lord's promise did not mean every Davidic king would be righteous.
It meant human rebellion would not ultimately defeat God's redemptive purpose.
Athaliah could attempt to destroy the royal family.
But she could not overthrow the God who had spoken.
And that is where the first whisper of grace enters this story.
Joash survived, not because he was strong, but because he was protected.
Before he ever wore a crown, somebody carried him to safety.
Before he ever gave an order, somebody risked everything to preserve his life.
And before he could even understand the covenant, he was living inside the consequences of God's faithfulness.
Some of us know something about that.
We look back over our lives and realize we survived situations we were not strong enough to handle.
There were doors we could not open.
Battles we could not win.
Dangers we did not even recognize.
And yet, by the mercy of God, we are still here.
But surviving by grace is not the same thing as responding faithfully to grace.
Joash's life would eventually prove that distinction in the most painful way imaginable.
When Joash was seven years old, Jehoiada arranged for him to be publicly crowned king.
The priest organized the necessary protection, brought out the young heir, placed the crown upon him, and presented the testimony associated with the kingship.
The people rejoiced.
Athaliah heard the celebration.
She rushed toward the commotion, saw the crowned boy, and cried out, "Treason!"
The irony is almost unbearable.
The woman who had seized power through bloodshed accused the rightful heir of betrayal.
Athaliah was removed and executed, and Jehoiada led a covenant renewal involving the Lord, the king, and the people.
The worship of Baal was confronted, and the temple of the Lord was restored to its proper place in the nation's life.
The little boy who had been hidden from death now sat on David's throne.
What a beginning.
What a testimony.
What a future he seemed to have.
Then Scripture gives us two verses that deserve far more attention than they usually receive.
Second Chronicles 24:2–3 says in the King James Version:
"And Joash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters."
Read those words again.
Especially the first sentence.
Joash did what was right in the sight of the Lord all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
That qualifying phrase matters.
In Hebrew, the text says:
"וַיַּעַשׂ יוֹאָשׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה כָּל־יְמֵי יְהוֹיָדָע הַכֹּהֵן"
Vayya'as Yo'ash hayyashar be'enei Adonai, kol-yemei Yehoyada hakkohen.
The meaning is straightforward:
"And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest."
The Hebrew expression kol-yemei Yehoyada means "all the days of Jehoiada."
The chronicler is not merely praising Joash.
He is preparing us for a contrast.
Because something terrible will happen after Jehoiada dies.
But first, the marriages.
The Hebrew of verse 3 reads:
"וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ יְהוֹיָדָע נָשִׁים שְׁתָּיִם וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת"
Vayyissa-lo Yehoyada nashim shettayim, vayyole(d) banim uvanot.
In context, the verse means:
"And Jehoiada took two wives for him, and he fathered sons and daughters."
The verb used here describes Jehoiada taking or obtaining wives on Joash's behalf.
The text does not say that Jehoiada married these women himself.
It says he obtained them for Joash.
And that raises the question.
Why?
Here is where we must be careful not to confuse a plausible historical explanation with something God has explicitly revealed.
Scripture does not tell us Jehoiada's private reasoning.
It does not name these two wives.
It does not describe their ages, family backgrounds, or personal relationships with Joash.
It does not tell us exactly when the marriages took place.
And it does not explicitly declare that God commanded Jehoiada to arrange two marriages.
What we can say is that these marriages occurred within the larger story of restoring and continuing the Davidic royal household.
Joash had narrowly escaped the destruction of the royal family.
He was the surviving heir through whom David's dynasty continued in Judah.
The birth of sons and daughters therefore carried obvious dynastic significance.
In the ancient royal world, marriages could strengthen a king's household, establish family relationships, and help secure succession.
It is reasonable to understand Jehoiada's action in that historical setting.
But it would go beyond Scripture to insist that political alliances were his specific motive, or that both marriages were directly commanded by God.
The Bible simply does not say.
And that distinction matters.
Because we must never make Scripture say more than Scripture says, even when a dramatic explanation would make a story more exciting.
There is another difficult question.
Why two wives?
Does this mean God approved of polygamy?
Not necessarily.
The Bible often records actions without endorsing them.
Genesis 2:24 presents the foundational marriage pattern: a man united to his wife, the two becoming one flesh.
Jesus Himself returns to that creation design in Matthew 19:4–6.
And Deuteronomy 17:17 specifically warns Israel's kings against multiplying wives, lest their hearts turn away.
That warning becomes painfully relevant in the life of Solomon, whose many marriages contributed to his spiritual downfall.
At the same time, the Old Testament describes polygamous households as historical realities, sometimes without offering an immediate explicit condemnation of each individual arrangement.
Joash's two marriages are reported, but the passage does not identify them as either the cause of his later apostasy or an exemplary marriage model for believers.
We should not manufacture a condemnation the passage does not make.
Neither should we treat narrative description as permission to disregard God's design for marriage.
The deeper tragedy of Joash's life is not that Scripture mentions two wives.
It is that Scripture tells us he did right while Jehoiada lived.
And then tells us what happened when Jehoiada was gone.
This is where the story stops being merely about an ancient king.
It starts becoming uncomfortably personal.
Because some people are faithful as long as someone else is watching.
Some pray because their parents pray.
Some attend church because their spouse insists.
Some avoid certain sins because their pastor knows them.
Some appear spiritually strong because they are surrounded by spiritually strong people.
But what happens when the person who keeps reminding you of God is no longer there?
What happens when nobody is checking?
When the worship music stops?
When the church doors close?
When the mentor dies?
When the godly influence that shaped your life disappears?
Who are you then?
Joash was about to answer that question.
And the answer would break the heart of everyone who had hoped his story would end differently.
For years, Joash demonstrated concern for the temple.
Second Chronicles 24 describes his determination to repair the house of the Lord.
He confronted delays in the work and helped establish arrangements for collecting the necessary contributions.
The people responded.
Funds were gathered.
Workers repaired the temple.
The house of God was restored.
Can you picture the scene?
The sound of craftsmen at work.
The movement of people bringing contributions.
The damaged temple being repaired.
The young king who had once been hidden inside that sacred environment now helping restore it.
From the outside, everything looked beautiful.
A rescued king.
A respected priest.
A restored temple.
A nation returning to covenant worship.
If the story ended here, Joash might be remembered simply as one of Judah's great reforming kings.
But the Bible refuses to hide the rest.
Jehoiada grew old.
Very old.
According to 2 Chronicles 24:15, he died at the age of 130.
Scripture honors him as a man who had done good in Israel, toward God, and toward God's house.
He was buried among the kings in the City of David.
Think about the weight of that honor.
Jehoiada was not himself the reigning monarch.
Yet his service to God and the royal house was so significant that he received a burial associated with kings.
He had protected Joash as a child.
He had helped establish him on the throne.
He had led the people in covenant renewal.
He had stood beside the king through years of reform.
And now he was gone.
The man who had guarded Joash's childhood could no longer guard his choices.
Then comes one of the most devastating transitions in the entire account.
Second Chronicles 24:17–18 tells us that after Jehoiada's death, the princes of Judah came and bowed before the king.
Joash listened to them.
And the nation abandoned the house of the Lord, the God of their fathers, and served sacred poles and idols.
Let that settle.
The same king who had helped repair the temple now participated in abandoning the God worshiped there.
The same king whose life had been preserved through Jehoiada's courage now listened to voices leading him away from Jehoiada's faithful teaching.
The same man who had benefited from covenant faithfulness now became involved in covenant rebellion.
How does a person fall that far?
The text identifies a decisive change in influence.
But it does not give us permission to claim we know every secret thought in Joash's heart.
What it does show is enough.
His outward righteousness did not endure after his godly mentor's death.
And that should disturb us.
Because being close to holy things is not the same as having a heart that remains faithful to God.
You can know Christian language and still resist Christ.
You can participate in ministry and still refuse repentance.
You can help maintain a church building while neglecting obedience in your private life.
You can inherit a testimony without personally embracing the God who made that testimony possible.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility of all is this:
You can become so accustomed to appearing faithful that you stop examining whether you actually are.
But God did not immediately abandon Joash without warning.
Second Chronicles 24:19 says the Lord sent prophets to bring the people back to Him.
They testified against the nation.
But the people would not listen.
There is mercy even in that warning.
God confronted their rebellion before judgment fell.
He called them back.
He exposed the danger.
He gave them opportunity to turn.
And then the story becomes almost unbearable.
The Spirit of God clothed Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest.
The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 24:20 uses the striking expression:
"וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים לָבְשָׁה אֶת־זְכַרְיָה"
Ve-ruach Elohim laveshah et-Zekharyah.
Literally, the wording pictures the Spirit of God clothing Zechariah.
It communicates divine empowerment for the prophetic message he was about to deliver.
Zechariah stood before the people and confronted their disobedience.
He asked why they were transgressing the commandments of the Lord.
Then came the terrible warning:
"Because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you."
That is 2 Chronicles 24:20 in the King James Version.
The message was not an invitation to despair.
It was a truthful confrontation with covenant rebellion.
A warning that their abandonment of God would bring devastating consequences.
And who was delivering it?
The son of Jehoiada.
The son of the man who had helped save Joash's life.
The son of the priest who had crowned him.
The son of the man who had stood beside him when he was young and vulnerable.
If anyone's voice should have reminded Joash of mercy, surely it was this man's.
But instead of receiving correction, Joash allowed his heart to harden.
Second Chronicles 24:21 says the people conspired against Zechariah and stoned him with stones at the command of the king, in the court of the house of the Lord.
Read that slowly.
At the command of the king.
In the court of the house of the Lord.
The place associated with Joash's rescue and the worship he had helped restore became the setting for the murder of a prophet confronting his rebellion.
And verse 22 makes the betrayal unmistakable.
"Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son."
Here "his father" refers to Jehoiada, Zechariah's father.
The chronicler deliberately highlights Joash's ingratitude.
He forgot the kindness.
Not necessarily because the historical facts had vanished from his memory.
But because his actions utterly disregarded the mercy he had received.
And now the story becomes more than tragic.
It becomes a mirror.
Because how often do we receive mercy, then resent the very truth that calls us to remain faithful?
How often do we ask God to rescue us from consequences, then resist Him when He confronts the sin that led us there?
How often do we love encouragement but despise correction?
We want the God who opens doors.
But not always the God who tells us to turn around.
We want forgiveness.
But we do not always want repentance.
We want restoration.
But we resist surrender.
And when someone loves us enough to speak biblical truth, we sometimes treat that person as the enemy.
Joash's response was far more violent than ordinary resistance to correction.
But the warning reaches into every heart tempted to reject truth simply because truth hurts.
Zechariah died calling upon the Lord to see and require an account.
The king had silenced the messenger.
He had not silenced God.
Later, a relatively small Syrian force came against Judah, and the Lord gave Judah's larger army into their hands because the nation had forsaken Him.
Judgment fell.
Joash was severely wounded.
Then his own servants conspired against him and killed him.
Second Chronicles 24:25 explicitly connects their conspiracy to the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest.
The account ends with Joash buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
Think of the contrast.
Jehoiada, the priest who served faithfully, received burial among the kings.
Joash, the king who turned away, was denied that royal burial honor.
The man who had been given so much finished his life under the shadow of betrayal.
The rescued child became a compromised ruler.
The temple restorer became a persecutor of God's prophet.
The recipient of kindness became the author of cruelty.
And the boy who had been saved from murder eventually ordered the killing of the son of his protector.
There are endings that make you cry.
And then there are endings that make you examine your own soul.
This is one of them.
But we must not stop here.
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of Joash.
It is the story of God's redemptive purpose moving through broken human history toward Jesus Christ.
And the contrast between Joash and Jesus is breathtaking.
Joash was a son of David whose life was preserved from a murderous ruler.
Jesus, the greater Son of David, was also threatened by a murderous ruler in His childhood, when Herod sought to destroy the young child, as Matthew 2 records.
But their paths diverged.
Joash began well and turned away.
Jesus remained faithful to the Father, even unto death.
Joash rejected a prophet who confronted his sin.
Jesus was Himself rejected, though He was without sin.
Joash participated in the shedding of innocent blood.
Jesus willingly shed His own innocent blood to save sinners.
Joash depended on the guidance of a faithful priest and eventually abandoned that priest's teaching.
Jesus is our faithful and eternal High Priest, who never abandons His people.
Hebrews 7:25 says:
"Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."
That is our hope.
Not that we will always have a Jehoiada beside us.
Not that our Christian upbringing will automatically protect us from rebellion.
Not that our church attendance, ministry activity, or religious reputation can make us righteous.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
The One who lives forever.
The One whose priesthood does not end in death.
The One whose obedience does not collapse under pressure.
The One whose grace is sufficient for sinners who repent and come to Him in faith.
And perhaps this is where the story reaches you personally.
Because maybe you have not murdered a prophet.
Maybe you have not abandoned a temple.
Maybe you have never worn a crown.
But perhaps you recognize something of Joash's spiritual danger in yourself.
You were raised around Scripture, but your private relationship with God has grown cold.
You know what to say in church, but you have stopped being honest in prayer.
You remember when worship moved you to tears, but now your heart barely responds.
You once welcomed correction, but lately you become defensive whenever God's Word challenges you.
You are still doing Christian things.
But you know something has changed.
And the hardest part is that other people might not notice.
They still see the familiar smile.
The familiar Bible verses.
The familiar Sunday routine.
But God sees what happens when nobody else is watching.
He sees the compromises you have explained away.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The pride you refuse to confess.
The obedience you keep postponing.
And still, His Word calls you to return.
Not because your sin is small.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is not permission to keep sinning without concern.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend your past never happened.
It tells you that Christ died for sins and rose again, and that forgiveness and new life are found in Him.
The Gospel does not flatter your pride.
It crucifies your claim to self-sufficiency.
It tells the truth about your sin.
And then it announces a Savior greater than your sin.
They are not a promise that every earthly story will have an easy ending.
Joash's did not.
They are not a claim that consequences disappear whenever we say a prayer.
They do not.
They are a declaration that sin, shame, and human failure do not have the final authority over those who belong to Jesus Christ.
His death and resurrection open the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life.
But we must come to Him.
We must repent.
We must believe.
We must not confuse religious familiarity with saving faith.
And we must never presume that yesterday's obedience excuses today's rebellion.
The New Testament calls believers to perseverance, vigilance, and mutual encouragement.

Hebrews 3:12–13 warns against an evil heart of unbelief that departs from the living God, and urges believers to exhort one another daily so that none will be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
That is one reason Christian community matters.
Not because a pastor, mentor, spouse, or ministry can replace Christ.
But because God uses His Word and His people to encourage, correct, strengthen, and remind us of the Savior.
Jehoiada was a remarkable spiritual influence.
But no human mentor can be the permanent foundation of another person's faith.
Our foundation must be Christ Himself.
And this is why I want to ask you something more important than whether you understand Joash's marriages.
If every person who currently encourages your faith disappeared from your daily life, would you still follow Jesus?
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
But sincerely.
Would you still open your Bible?
Would you still pray when nobody praised you for praying?
Would you still turn from sin when nobody threatened to expose you?
Would you still love Christ when obedience cost you something?
Or would the absence of human accountability reveal that you had been following the expectations of people more than the Lord?
Please do not rush past that question.
It may be the most important question you carry out of this story.
And if the answer frightens you, do not respond by pretending.
Respond by coming to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess the distance.
Confess the compromise.
Ask Him to search your heart.
Ask Him to teach you obedience that is rooted in love for Him, not merely fear of disappointing others.
The Lord is not impressed by a performance of righteousness.
He calls us to genuine faith and repentance.
And He is merciful to those who come to Him through His Son.
If this story exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your sin for strangers to read.
And if you have experienced God's mercy after wandering away, consider sharing a brief testimony of His faithfulness.
Someone reading the comments may be quietly wondering whether it is too late for them to return.
Your words might remind them to seek the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
There is another way this story should move us.
It should make us grateful for faithful spiritual influences without turning those people into idols.
Perhaps there was a mother who prayed over you.
A father who opened the Bible with you.
A pastor who corrected you when you were drifting.
A friend who refused to encourage your compromise.
A grandparent whose faithfulness left an imprint on your soul.
Perhaps that person is still alive.
Perhaps they are already with the Lord.
Do not wait until they are gone to recognize the value of their faithfulness.
If this article brought someone to mind, consider tagging them with a simple word of gratitude.
Or send it privately with a message saying, "Thank you for pointing me toward Jesus."
A family member may need the warning.
A friend may need the encouragement.
A weary believer may need to remember that Jesus is still worthy of following.
A person who has never understood the Gospel may encounter the truth of Christ through something you share.
You do not know every heart that will read it.
But you can be faithful with the opportunity you have.
Not because an article can replace Scripture, but because the warning of Joash is worth revisiting.
Especially when life becomes comfortable.
Especially when your spiritual disciplines become mechanical.
Especially when you begin to assume that being around Christianity is the same as walking with Christ.
There is room here for honest questions, biblical encouragement, repentance, and the pursuit of a deeper understanding of God's Word.
And if this ministry has genuinely strengthened your faith, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
Not because a monthly payment earns God's favor.
And certainly not because you must pay money to glorify God.
You can glorify God through faithful obedience, generosity, prayer, love, and service in countless ways.
But supporting trustworthy Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of Christian stewardship.
It is not a replacement for the biblical responsibilities you prayerfully recognize toward your local church, your family, and those in need.
Nor should anyone give out of fear, pressure, or a promise of financial blessing.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
If the Lord has provided for you and you believe in this work, your ongoing support can help us reach more people with the message of Christ.
It can help sustain the writing, preparation, and sharing of biblical resources.
It can help us keep reminding people that the answer to sin is not religious performance, but repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Those products are not the heart of this mission.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for personal reflection, and opportunities to share faith in everyday life.
Those free resources are part of the mission, too.
Because biblical nourishment should not be reduced to a transaction.
Our desire is to help people read Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, and follow Christ more faithfully.
A faithful ministry is not measured merely by the number of paying supporters.
It must be measured by faithfulness to Christ and His Word.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a kingdom around a personality.
It is to point people toward the King whose kingdom will never end.
The King greater than Joash.
The King greater than David.
The King who does not need another priest to keep Him faithful.
The King who is Himself our perfect High Priest.
The King who was crowned with thorns, crucified for sinners, and raised in victory.
Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, remember the little boy.
Remember the child hidden from a murderous queen.
Remember the priest who risked so much to protect him.
Remember the crown.
Remember the restored temple.
Remember the two marriages that helped continue his royal household.
Remember the sons and daughters.
Remember the years of outward faithfulness.
Then remember the grave of Jehoiada.
The flattering voices.
The abandoned worship.
The prophet standing before the people.
The stones.
The blood.
The betrayal.
And remember that Scripture did not preserve this account merely to satisfy our curiosity about ancient royal marriages.

It preserved a sobering testimony about covenant unfaithfulness, the danger of rejecting God's correction, and the difference between being surrounded by righteousness and persevering in genuine devotion to God.
The story asks us to examine our own hearts.
But the Gospel directs us beyond ourselves.
To the Savior who is faithful when we are weak.
To the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
To the Savior who forgives and transforms those who come to Him.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, do not merely ask whether you have been raised around the right people.
Ask whether you are following the right King.
Do not merely ask whether your life looks Christian from the outside.
Ask whether you are trusting and obeying Christ from the heart.
Do not merely thank God for the Jehoiadas He has placed in your life.
Thank Him for Jesus, the eternal High Priest who is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him.
And if you have wandered, do not make another excuse.
Turn to Christ.
His grace is not an invitation to remain in rebellion.
It is the mercy that calls you out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Because the greatest tragedy is not losing the person who taught you to follow God. It is discovering that you never learned to follow Him when that person was gone.
